prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit ubiquitin ligases to destroy proteins that cannot be blocked, from the first PROTACs to the cereblon-mediated molecular-glue action of thalidomide-class drugs.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize for targeted protein degradation (B044) with Crews, Deshaies and Handa. It is the only configuration with explicit multi-member support (four of eight) and every member lists it somewhere, but I rest the case on the science rather than the count. The principle is simple and quantitatively explicit: a small molecule induces proximity between a target and an E3 ligase, so pharmacology becomes event-driven and catalytic rather than occupancy-driven, and ternary-complex cooperativity gives a measurable design rule. It opens a capability that was not foreseen, reaching proteins with no active site to block, it has been reproduced across many ligases, targets and laboratories, and it can be explained to a broad audience. On the chair's question of one achievement or two, I hold that the unifying discovery is the exploitation of the ubiquitin ligase machinery by small molecules. Crews and Deshaies established that a designed bifunctional molecule can do it, and Handa showed that nature and medicine already did it, in thalidomide-class drugs acting through cereblon. The citation is worded to say that the two routes converge on one mechanism and does not claim cereblon work as PROTAC chemistry.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC drug is approved to my knowledge, and none of the first-round files verifies this independently, so clinical vindication of the bifunctional branch is incomplete. Handa's contribution is chiefly target identification, and Somfai's question about what was chemically new there is fair: the added value is the mechanistic explanation that makes the molecular-glue branch intelligible, not new bond-forming chemistry. Ciulli (VHL ligands, ternary-complex structures), Sakamoto, Gray, Ito and Kim are left out by the three-person cap, and Chabes's Crews-and-Deshaies reading is cleaner on attribution but leaves the clinically most validated branch without its mechanistic anchor. The citation also risks sounding like two discoveries stapled together. I accept these costs because I see no alternative on the shortlist that is both mature and broadly supported.

responses.point: Chabes proposes a two-part prize, base editing for Liu alone and degradation for Crews and Deshaies, as two general chemical-biology tools, and would give Handa a place only in a single-achievement configuration.
responses.response: I do not find the pairing coherent as a prize. The two parts share a style of argument, turning a biological outcome into a defined chemical event, but not a common achievement, and the Liu-alone credit is contested by five members including me because Komor and Gaudelli made the decisive cytosine and adenine editor experiments and Kondo and Nishida report independent priority. I take your chemistry argument about CRISPR overlap seriously, and I keep B019 as an alternative, but I would not build a two-part prize on a sole credit I cannot defend. On Handa versus a Crews-and-Deshaies-only reading, I stay with Handa: without cereblon the glue branch has no explained mechanism, and your own uncertainty list asks whether he should be in the degradation part.

responses.point: Aili ranks B044 first, names Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and argues that independent reproduction and the established mechanism matter more than drug approval, with Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto left out by the cap.
responses.response: We agree on the trio and on the weight of approval, and your argument that the mechanism is established regardless of approval persuades me more than it did in round 1. I would answer the lay-audience problem by letting the citation carry the principle, hijacking ubiquitin ligases, and by recognising that the cap is a cost. I still want the committee to be explicit that Handa is credited for cereblon as the thalidomide target and Crews and Deshaies for the PROTAC concept, so that Ciulli's omission rests on that division of credit, not on seniority.

responses.point: Aqvist moved from Ciulli to Handa after the openings but notes that dropping Ciulli is a real cost, and that the PROTAC and cereblon strands have different intellectual origins, so one citation risks being vague or unfair.
responses.response: Your point about different intellectual origins is the strongest argument against my citation, and I have no complete answer. My position is that the shared mechanism is the discovery that survives scrutiny, and a citation naming the recruitment of ubiquitin ligases by small molecules is more accurate than two parts that would have to be limited to one or two names each under the cap. If you can show that Ciulli's structural basis for ternary complexes is the step that turned PROTACs from a concept into a design discipline, I would reconsider the third name, but that evidence has not been put in front of me.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers nitrogenase for Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt on the grounds of three decades of confirmed structures, while conceding that the catalytic cycle is not settled.
responses.response: I share your taste for a physically explicit mechanism, and the FeMo-cofactor structure is a firm achievement. But you concede that the E4 state, the substrate-binding site and the order of proton and electron delivery are open, and I cannot write a citation that stays on the structure without implying an answer to how N2 is reduced. Unless you can show that a structure-and-cofactor citation can be framed without that implication, I would keep B032 behind degradation, though not as an unreasonable candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Sparr prefers phase separation for Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as a physical-chemical principle of cellular organisation, and admits it may not reach five votes.
responses.response: I ranked B039 fourth and have not changed my view that the thermodynamic framework is important. The condensate question I raised in round 1, which in-cell condensates are true equilibrium phases and which predictions are confirmed in living cells rather than in vitro, has not been answered in your statement, so I still treat it as a maturity problem rather than a flaw in the science.

uncertainties: Whether one degradation citation can state the unifying ligase-recruitment principle without implying that Handa's cereblon work is PROTAC chemistry.
Whether Handa or Ciulli is the better third name beside Crews and Deshaies, given Sakamoto, Gray, Ito and Kim are also omitted.
Whether the absence of an approved PROTAC drug, which no file has verified, makes the prize premature this year.
Whether the five-vote majority can be reached by any configuration, since the other preferred parts each have one supporter.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the credited names in B044 or the alternatives. As chair, I note that nanopore sensing (B068) and phase separation (B039) lie near my nanophysics and biophysics interests, and I continue to share a Lund affiliation with committee colleagues Somfai and Sparr. My opening first choice, B068, drew no support from others and I keep it only as an alternative. Nothing has changed since round 1.
